The sessions covered key aspects of maritime safety and regulatory compliance, including practical implementation of the International Safety Management (ISM) Code, assessment of ISM and Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) compliance, and the evolving role of Port State Control in strengthening preventive safety measures.

A panel discussion on “High-Performance Horizons for Indian Maritime” provided a platform for deliberations on enhancing safety performance and operational standards across the maritime sector.

The workshop also featured an industry-focused session titled “Voices from the Fleet: Real-World Safety Compliance and Near-Miss Realities”, with participation from The Great Eastern Shipping Co. Ltd., The Shipping Corporation of India Ltd., Seven Islands Shipping Ltd. and Apeejay Shipping Ltd., bringing industry perspectives on operational safety, compliance challenges and near-miss reporting.

The technical sessions underscored the importance of effective safety management, proactive compliance and continued collaboration between maritime regulators, recognised organisations and shipping companies in strengthening India's maritime safety ecosystem.

The Canaanite palace complex at Tel Megiddo in northern Israel was a massive Middle and Late Bronze Age royal center (dating roughly to the 2nd millennium BCE) that reflected the city-state's great wealth, strategic importance along the Via Maris trade route, and strong commercial and political ties with Egypt. 

Key Features and Architecture
Layout and Structure: The palace complex centered around large open courtyards surrounded by heavy stone-walled rooms (with walls measuring roughly 2 meters thick), storehouses, and service areas. 
Lesser Canaanite Palace: A secondary smaller palace structure within the complex featured a large courtyard and fixed stone basins, demonstrating that royal Megiddo functioned as an expansive administrative compound rather than just a single standalone building. 
Monumental Gateway: A large northern gate complex featuring massive ashlar masonry and trimmed basalt foundations provided direct chariot and ceremonial access to the palace and city. 
Egyptian Administration: During the 15th through 13th centuries BCE, Megiddo served as a major Canaanite royal seat and a key administrative/logistical base for Egyptian rule in Canaan. 

Major Archaeological Discoveries
The Canaanite Palace Treasury: Excavations yielded rare luxury items, including intricate gold jewelry, bronze-age Baal figurines, and fine carved ivory plaques, illustrating the high status of the city's rulers. 
The 3,600-Year-Old Royal Tomb: An undisturbed underground burial chamber discovered directly adjacent to the Middle Bronze Age royal palace contained high-status remains—including a 40-to-60-year-old man wearing a gold diadem and torque, a woman in her 30s, an 8-to-10-year-old child, and earlier jumbled burials—accompanied by Cypriot ceramic vessels, Egyptian stone jars, and gold and silver jewelry. 

Tel Megiddo (from Hebrew: תל מגידו; Arabic: تل المتسلم, Tell el-Muteselim) is the site of the ancient city of Megiddo (/məˈɡɪdoʊ/; Hebrew: מגידו; Greek: Μεγιδδώ), the remains of which form a tell or archaeological mound, situated in northern Israel at the western edge of the Jezreel Valley. During the Bronze Age, Megiddo was an important Canaanite city-state, and in the Iron Age, it became a royal city in the Kingdom of Israel. The site is renowned for its historical, geographical, and theological significance, especially under its Greek name Armageddon (Ἁρμαγεδών), which appears once in the Koine Greek New Testament in Revelation 16:16.

Excavations have unearthed 20 strata of ruins since the Neolithic phase, indicating a long settlement period.[1] Occupied continuously from the early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the Persian period (c. 332 BCE), Megiddo was strategically located at the crossroads of major ancient trade routes, making it a key center for trade, politics, and military affairs. Excavations have uncovered impressive fortifications, including massive city walls and gates, as well as palaces, temples, residential buildings, and a sophisticated water system. The site is protected as Megiddo National Park and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[2]

For centuries, Christians have revered the woman chosen by God to bear the Savior of the world. Her story is one of courage, faith, and obedience—a life central to God’s redemptive plan. Yet to fully comprehend her role as Jesus’ mother, it helps to look beyond the familiar name of “Mary” and rediscover her true identity, including through her genealogy, as “Miriam.”
Miriam’s Hebrew name roots her in the history and covenantal promises of Israel. It connects her to her people’s struggles and the hope embodied in the prophecies about the coming of the Messiah.
What can her story and heritage reveal about Mary’s role as the mother of Jesus? And how does it transform the way we see, and apply, God’s promises today?

Miriam or Mary? (or Maria?)
While some question whether Mary and Miriam are the same name, there are important linguistic and historical factors we need to consider.

The New Testament was written in Greek, and many of the names were translated or transliterated from Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek. The Hebrew name “Miriam” became Miryam or Maryam in Aramaic.
Jesus and his contemporaries would have spoken Aramaic, a language closely related to Hebrew. The Gospels use the form Maria, which then became Mary in English. Since Greek female names often end in -a/-ah, and that is likely how Maryam became Marya.

It is worth noting that the name “Miriam” was prominent in the land of the Bible, and it is not surprising that several women were named Mary/Maryam/Miriam in Jesus’ circles. It confirms the popularity of the name among Jewish women of the time.

Interestingly, while the Western churches use the name Mary or Maria for the mother of Jesus, the Eastern Orthodox Church still often refers to her as “Miriam” in their liturgy.

Le 15 octobre 1894, Alfred Dreyfus était arrêté pour trahison. Cent trente-deux ans plus tard, l’Affaire nous rappelle une vérité dérangeante : une institution peut finir par défendre son mensonge au nom même de son honneur.

Dreyfus était capitaine dans l’armée française, alsacien, patriote et juif. Accusé d’avoir transmis des secrets militaires à l’Allemagne, il fut condamné sur la base d’un dossier fragile, dans un climat profondément marqué par l’antisémitisme. Dégradé publiquement, puis envoyé au bagne de l’île du Diable, il allait devenir le symbole d’une injustice qui déchira la France. Mais ce qui me frappe le plus dans cette histoire, ce n’est pas seulement l’erreur judiciaire initiale. C’est l’obstination avec laquelle des hommes parfaitement capables de reconnaître la vérité préférèrent protéger le prestige de l’armée.

Lorsque des éléments accablants commencèrent à désigner un autre officier, Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy, la question aurait dû être simple : un innocent avait-il été condamné? Elle devint pourtant une question de loyauté institutionnelle. Reconnaître l’erreur, pensait-on, reviendrait à affaiblir l’armée, à humilier la nation et à donner des armes à ses adversaires. C’est ainsi que l’honneur, détaché de la vérité, finit par devenir son contraire. 

Pour nous, catholiques, l’Affaire Dreyfus comporte aussi une dimension particulièrement douloureuse. Une partie importante de la presse catholique française participa à la campagne antidreyfusarde, parfois avec une violence antisémite difficile à lire aujourd’hui. Certains présentèrent même la défense de Dreyfus comme une attaque contre la France chrétienne.

Il serait injuste d’en conclure que tous les catholiques partageaient ces positions. Des voix catholiques défendirent la justice et refusèrent de sacrifier la vérité aux passions politiques. Mais il serait tout aussi malhonnête de minimiser la responsabilité de ceux qui utilisèrent leur identité religieuse pour légitimer une injustice. Et c’est précisément là que cette histoire conserve toute sa force.

La fidélité à une institution, qu’il s’agisse de l’armée, de la nation ou même de l’Église, ne saurait jamais nous dispenser de notre devoir envers la vérité. Au contraire, plus une institution est digne d’être aimée, plus nous devons vouloir qu’elle soit juste. Un catholique ne défend pas l’Église en excusant systématiquement les fautes de ceux qui exercent l’autorité en son sein. Il la sert en refusant que son autorité soit séparée de la vérité et de la justice.

Cela ne signifie pas que toute accusation soit fondée, ni que la défiance envers les institutions soit une vertu. Dreyfus lui-même nous rappelle combien la présomption d’innocence, la rigueur des preuves et le respect des procédures sont essentiels. Mais lorsqu’une institution découvre qu’elle s’est trompée, sa grandeur ne consiste pas à préserver les apparences. Elle consiste à reconnaître l’erreur et à réparer l’injustice. En 1906, après douze années de combats judiciaires et politiques, Alfred Dreyfus fut finalement réhabilité. Cette victoire fut celle de la justice, mais elle arriva après des années de souffrance qu’aucune décision de justice ne pouvait effacer.

Je crois que l’Affaire Dreyfus nous enseigne quelque chose de profondément chrétien : la vérité ne devient pas moins vraie parce qu’elle embarrasse ceux auxquels nous sommes attachés. Et une fidélité qui exige de fermer les yeux sur l’injustice n’est plus véritablement une fidélité. Elle devient une forme d’idolâtrie.

Cent trente-deux ans après son arrestation, l’histoire de Dreyfus nous oblige encore à nous poser une question inconfortable : lorsque la vérité menace le prestige de notre propre camp, avons-nous le courage de la défendre ?

Growth Drivers & Expansion Plans
Shilchar Technologies’ growth opportunities are supported by rising global electricity demand, limited transformer supply, investment in ageing transmission and distribution infrastructure, renewable energy development, and industrial capital expenditure. Its investor presentation identifies an FY27 order pipeline of approximately ₹800 crore and highlights the potential for further capital expenditure depending on industry demand. The company’s Phase 3 expansion is expected to add 6,500 MVA, increasing installed capacity from 7,500 MVA to 14,000 MVA, with commissioning targeted for April 2027. During the earnings call, management stated that civil foundation work had been completed, equipment had been ordered, and the project remained on track. Management expects the new facility to support the next phase of growth from FY28 onwards. It also disclosed the purchase of additional land for potential future expansion, without specifying the eventual capacity or product mix.

Client Base
Shilchar Technologies serves domestic and international customers across renewable energy, power generation, electricity distribution, and industrial applications. Its customers require customised transformers for solar and wind power projects, hydroelectric installations, steel plants, and power distribution networks. The company exports to markets including North America, the Middle East, and parts of Africa, while also increasing its focus on domestic orders. During the August 2026 earnings call, management reported an order book of approximately ₹500 crore, comprising around 70% domestic orders and 30% export orders. Management explained that the geographic mix could change depending on shipping costs and developments in West Asia. The company’s focus on product quality, service, and lead times supports its positioning in specialised transformer markets.

Product Portfolio
Shilchar Technologies offers a range of transformers designed for different power generation, distribution, and industrial applications. Its portfolio includes power transformers used at the point of power generation and distribution transformers used in electricity distribution networks. It also manufactures inverter-duty transformers for solar power projects, generator transformers for wind power projects, hydro transformers used alongside turbines, and furnace transformers for steel plants. The investor presentation lists voltage classes of up to 66 kV for power transformers, 33 kV for distribution, inverter-duty, generator, and furnace transformers, and 132 kV for hydro transformers. The company is also expanding into the 220 kV class, extending its capabilities towards higher-voltage transformer applications.

3. SHILCHAR TECH.

Business Overview
Shilchar Technologies Limited manufactures power and distribution transformers, specialising in customised products for renewable energy and industrial applications. Its business covers transformers for power generation, electricity distribution, solar and wind projects, hydroelectric power, and industrial applications such as steel plants. The company follows a made-to-order manufacturing approach supported by in-house design and engineering capabilities, testing infrastructure, and a focus on order fulfilment. Its flagship manufacturing facility is located at Gavasad, Vadodara, and the company exports transformers to more than 25 countries across five continents. According to the Q1 FY27 investor presentation, its existing installed capacity was 7,500 MVA, with an additional 6,500 MVA planned through expansion. For Q1 FY27, revenue from operations was ₹134.61 crore and profit after tax was ₹20.86 crore.

Reliance, BSE Lead MF Buys in Sept: Mutual Funds Pour Nearly ₹6,000 Cr into Reliance Industries Ahead of Jio IPO, BSE Draws Over ₹5,500 Cr

Core Theme: 
Mutual funds backed Reliance and BSE most heavily in September, driven by the upcoming Jio IPO and BSE’s Nifty 50 entry, with banks and Swiggy also in favour, while large IT and industrial names such as Wipro, L&T and TCS saw the heaviest net selling.

Most-Bought Stocks: Top of the List
Reliance Industries emerged as the most-bought stock by mutual funds (MFs) in September, with net buying of nearly ₹6,000 crore (₹5,986 crore per chart)

Buying came ahead of the much-anticipated IPO of its subsidiary, Jio Platforms

BSE attracted net MF investments of more than ₹5,500 crore (₹5,609 crore per chart)

BSE was included in the benchmark Nifty 50 index on September 30

BSE buying was boosted by a block deal on the same day, in which MFs bought a bulk of the shares sold by Goldman Sachs and BNP Paribas

#SejalGlassLtd: 6 Industry Shifts Creating Opportunities

Sejal Glass Ltd is an architectural glass processor trying to move beyond conventional glass processing into higher-value, specialised products. Its opportunity lies at the intersection of India's premium construction market, energy-efficient buildings and the Gulf's architectural glass demand. But the big question is whether these tailwinds can translate into sustainable profitability.

Sejal buys basic float glass and converts it into toughened glass, laminated glass, insulated glass units (IGUs), printed glass and other customised products. In FY26, it generated ₹396.5 crore in revenue, with approximately 70% coming from its UAE business, which contributes almost all the group's profit.

6 INDUSTRY STRUCTURAL CHANGES BENEFITING SEJAL GLASS

1. India's safety-glass regulations are raising entry requirements. India's Safety Glass Quality Control Order requires applicable architectural toughened and laminated glass to comply with the relevant Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) requirements and carry the required ISI mark. As enforcement strengthens, compliant, organised processors may gain an advantage over uncertified competitors. Sejal already operates in this regulated market. However, certification is an entry requirement, not a unique competitive advantage; other capable processors can also obtain it.

2. Buildings are shifting towards energy efficiency. Premium residential projects, commercial offices and modern buildings increasingly require better thermal performance and safety. This supports demand for insulated glass units (IGUs), which use multiple panes separated by a sealed gap, and laminated glass, which helps hold glass together when broken. Sejal is already positioned in this trend: IGUs contributed approximately ₹279 crore, or 70.3% of FY26 revenue. The opportunity is to grow alongside demand without sacrificing margins to competition.

3. The Gulf construction market is driving demand. Residential towers, commercial buildings and large construction projects require substantial quantities of processed glass. Sejal's UAE manufacturing facility places it close to regional customers and project sites. Glass is often installed late in a construction project, so earlier project launches can generate demand for processors several years later. This supports near-term growth, but construction remains cyclical: slower property launches and excess supply can eventually reduce orders.

4. War-related shipping disruption is temporarily favouring local processors. The freight costs into the Gulf rose to roughly 3–5 times pre-war levels following the 2026 Iran-war disruption. More expensive and difficult shipping can make imported glass less competitive, benefiting local processors such as Sejal. However, this is a temporary supply advantage—not a permanent moat. If shipping normalises, imported glass could become competitive again and put pressure on local prices and margins.

5. Railway modernisation is opening another market. New coaches and upgrades create demand for glazing that meets railway-specific technical requirements. Sejal is an approved vendor for Integral Coach Factory (ICF), Chennai; Rail Coach Factory (RCF), Kapurthala; and Modern Coach Factory (MCF), Raebareli. These approvals create an opportunity to win railway orders, but railway-grade glass still represents less than 1% of sales in the period examined. The opportunity is real; its financial importance remains small.

6. Chinese glass supply presents both an opportunity and a threat. Oversupply of basic float glass can reduce input costs for processors. However, cheap Chinese processing equipment can also make it easier for competitors to add capacity. Sejal operates between powerful glass suppliers and customers who frequently negotiate project prices. Lower input costs therefore do not automatically translate into higher profits; Sejal must retain some of the benefit rather than pass it on through lower selling prices.

NOW COMES THE COMPANY'S OWN TRANSFORMATION

Sejal acquired a UAE glass-processing facility in 2023, establishing a substantial presence in the Gulf. In April 2025, it acquired two Indian plants from Glasstech Industries, expanding manufacturing capacity and product capabilities. These acquisitions have increased scale, but the Indian operations are yet to demonstrate attractive operating returns.

The most interesting new opportunity is fire-rated glass. Sejal has licensed polymer-gel technology and installed a production line in the UAE. Fire-rated glass can be used in fire doors, partitions and escape routes, subject to the relevant performance standards and approvals. If commercial production, certification and customer adoption succeed, this could help Sejal move into a more specialised product category. But a licensed technology and installed production line are not the same as a profitable business.

Sejal is also expanding its capabilities in digitally printed glass, façade panels, railway glazing and bullet-resistant products. These initiatives could diversify its revenue beyond standard glass processing. Yet the estimates specialty products contribute less than 2% of revenue, while reported R&D expenditure was nil in FY26. The transformation is therefore still unproven.

WHAT INVESTORS MUST WATCH

Three developments will determine whether this story becomes a stronger long-term business:

Can the UAE operation sustain healthy margins after construction demand and shipping conditions normalise?

Can the Indian facilities increase utilisation and improve operating profitability?

Can fire-rated and other specialised products generate meaningful revenue, attractive margins and cash flow?

My conclusion: Sejal Glass has credible growth opportunities, but an expanding market, new capacity and a specialty-product pipeline do not automatically create a durable competitive advantage. The real transformation will be proven when the company converts these opportunities into sustained margins, stronger cash generation and measurable revenue from specialised products.

Watch the economics, not just the expansion story.

Transformers: Manufacturing capacity is only the starting point

Transformers help change voltage levels so electricity can be transmitted and distributed efficiently.

However, not all transformers are the same. Distribution transformers, power transformers and specialised high-voltage equipment require different engineering capabilities and customer approvals.

Shilchar Technologies illustrates this opportunity.

According to its FY26 report:

🔹 Existing annual manufacturing capacity: 7,500 MVA.

🔹 Existing capability: Up to 50 MVA and the 132 kV class.

🔹 Planned capacity expansion: To 14,000 MVA.

🔹 Planned entry into the 220 kV class, with commissioning targeted for April 2027, subject to the relevant development and approval process.

But announced capacity is only one part of the story.

The company must qualify its products, secure orders, manufacture and deliver equipment profitably, and collect the resulting revenue.

Also, manufacturing capacity in MVA should not be confused with installed grid transformation capacity measured in GVA.

The real test is whether additional capacity translates into profitable sales and cash flow.

PROTEAN: Beyond De Novo Generation — Can LLM Agents Perform Text-Guided Protein Structure Editing?

1. PROTEAN introduces a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing, targeting the real protein-engineering setting: start from an existing protein and perform local, instruction-driven backbone edits while preserving the rest of the scaffold under strict conservation contracts.

2. The benchmark operationalizes a two-stage “LLM + generative backend” pipeline: an LLM acts as a constraint compiler that translates natural-language intent into backend-specific geometric constraints, then a 3D generative engine executes backbone remodeling.

3. PROTEAN contains 380 sub-tasks spanning eight edit types (six intervention families): helix enrichment, sheet enrichment, inter-domain approach, inter-domain separation, reference-fragment mimicry, core burial (shape/compaction), head-to-tail cyclization, and motif scaffolding (variable-length carrier design around fixed motifs).

4. A key contribution is the decoupled evaluation harness with multi-gated scoring: Tier 1 geometric compliance separates (G1) target attainment from (G3) off-target scope fidelity (i.e., did the method avoid collateral drift outside the edit region), while Tier 2 (G2) biophysical realizability tests redesign-and-refold consistency using ProteinMPNN (inverse folding) plus ESMFold (orthogonal refolding).

5. The benchmark enforces explicit edit scopes and hard preservation rules (e.g., protected residues must keep identity; length-preserving tasks disallow indels and non-canonical residues), turning “localized editing” into a contract-driven task rather than unconstrained regeneration.

6. In benchmarking, five frontier LLMs are paired with three heterogeneous backends (BoltzGen, ODesign, RFdiffusion3). Under joint geometric compliance (G1 ∧ G3, pass@16) for in-scaffold editing, the best agent-backend pairing reaches 46.0%, showing the task is feasible but far from solved.

7. The results highlight where difficulty comes from: ablations suggest LLM constraint compilation is often accurate, while the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage (unintended changes in protected scaffolds) and downstream refolding failure (edited backbones that do not self-consistently refold after sequence redesign).

8. Task-level diagnostics reveal distinct failure modes: helix enrichment is consistently easier than sheet enrichment (local i→i+4 hydrogen bonding vs. non-local strand pairing/registry); reference-fragment mimicry is highly discriminative because it requires correct residue mapping plus rigid-body geometric matching under preservation constraints.

9. Head-to-tail cyclization exposes a fundamental “Pareto deadlock” under strict preservation: models can often satisfy cyclization geometry and (separately) preserve scope, but cannot satisfy both simultaneously because ring closure induces unavoidable relaxation that violates the hard scaffold RMSD tolerance, yielding 0.0% joint success in the reported strict setting.

10. For motif scaffolding (de novo carrier around fixed motifs), success is defined strictly by G1 ∧ G2 ∧ G3; at s@16, top systems reach ~43–47% refolding-consistent success, and errors often trace to “linker arithmetic” (choosing linker lengths that avoid torsional strain and enable foldable global topology).

Chemical plants older than 20 years must upgrade, rebuild or shut down between 2026 and 2029.
On August 15, China's new Ecological and Environmental Code came into effect, bringing around 30 environmental laws into one framework.
In September, China also proposed stricter safety rules for nitration plants. These plants use risky chemical reactions to manufacture products used in dyes and pesticides. Factories failing certain safety requirements could face closure.
But remember, not every Chinese restriction benefits India.
For example, China also restricted fertiliser exports. Since India imports fertilisers, this can actually increase our costs.

Even PVC lost its export tax refund, but China still has too much production capacity. So removing the refund doesn't automatically mean prices will rise.

Now let's look at H-acid, where things are getting interesting.

H-acid is an important chemical used to manufacture textile dyes.

On March 19, 2026, an explosion occurred at a Chinese H-acid manufacturing plant.

Look at what happened to prices in China.

January: 40,000 yuan per tonne
April 9: 61,000 yuan
April 17: 67,500 yuan
August 28: 95,000 yuan
Mid-September: 130,000 to 150,000 yuan

That's more than 3X in less than a year.

Some sellers even quoted 200,000 yuan, although these were asking prices, not confirmed transaction prices.
Notice something important.
Prices were already rising before China's proposed September safety rules.
The factory explosion and supply shortages started the rally. The new regulations could add further pressure on supply.
And Indian companies are already seeing the impact.

Kiri Industries told analysts in August that its H-acid prices increased from ₹350-400/kg to ₹800-900/kg.

Look at Q1 FY27 results compared to Q1 FY26.

Kiri Industries:
Revenue increased from ₹202 Cr to ₹312 Cr. Operating margin improved from a negative 8% to a positive 5%.

Its factories were operating at around 60% capacity, meaning it still has room to increase production.

AksharChem:
Revenue increased from ₹97 Cr to ₹141 Cr. Operating margin improved from 7% to 16%.

Bodal Chemicals:
Operating profit increased from ₹48 Cr to ₹69 Cr, but its margin remained around 10%.

One reason is that Bodal uses much of its own H-acid to manufacture dyes, instead of selling all of it directly.

Also remember, higher H-acid prices are good for manufacturers selling H-acid, but bad for dye manufacturers who need to buy it.

So the same chemical price increase can benefit one company and hurt another.
Here's what I'm watching now.

China is allowing older factories to upgrade their facilities instead of permanently shutting them down.

If these factories return with even larger production capacity, we could see the same situation as 2019.
Prices rise, Indian companies benefit temporarily, and then cheap Chinese supply returns.

Also, the new nitration safety rules are still in draft form.
My recommendation:

I'm closely tracking Kiri Industries, AksharChem and Bodal Chemicals.

But I wouldn't blindly buy chemical stocks just because China is tightening environmental rules.

I prefer companies that already have manufacturing capacity available, can increase production quickly and are benefiting from higher selling prices.

The biggest thing to track is whether Chinese factories are permanently closing or simply upgrading.

Because that will decide whether this chemical cycle lasts for years or ends like the previous one.

Not investment advice. Just sharing how I'm understanding this cycle.
